content: Galanthus, commonly known as snowdrop, is a genus of approximately 20 species of bulbous, herbaceous perennials belonging to the Amaryllis family. The name derives from the Greek words gála, meaning milk, and ánthos, meaning flower, referencing the white color of the blooms. Most species of Galanthus flower during the winter months, prior to the vernal equinox, although some species bloom in early spring or late autumn. Snowdrops are often mistaken for related genera within the Galantheae tribe, such as Leucojum (snowflakes) and Acis. All Galanthus species are perennial plants that grow from bulbs. Each bulb typically produces two or three linear leaves and a single, leafless flowering stalk (scape). At the top of the scape, a pair of bract-like spathe valves, joined by a thin papery membrane, encloses the developing flower. The flower itself is solitary, pendulous, and bell-shaped, with a white coloration. It is borne on a slender pedicel and lacks true petals. Instead, the flower is composed of six tepals, with the outer three being larger and more convex than the inner three. The six anthers release pollen through pores or short slits, and the ovary is divided into three chambers, maturing into a three-celled capsule. The seeds, which are whitish and possess a fleshy appendage called an elaiosome, attract ants that aid in seed dispersal. After flowering, the leaves die back within a few weeks. A distinguishing feature of Galanthus species is the green or greenish-yellow markings on the inner tepals, often forming a bridge-like shape over the small notch (sinus) at the tip of each tepal. Another key characteristic used to differentiate species and hybrids is the arrangement of the emerging leaves, known as vernation. Vernation can be classified as applanate (leaves pressed flat against each other), explicative (leaves pressed flat but with edges folded back or rolled), or supervolute (one leaf tightly clasped around the other). Notable species include: Galanthus nivalis (Common Snowdrop): Grows to a height of 7–15 cm and flowers between January and April in the northern temperate zone. It exhibits applanate vernation. Galanthus plicatus (Crimean Snowdrop): Reaches up to 30 cm in height, flowers from January to March, and has broad leaves with edges folded back (explicative vernation). Galanthus elwesii (Giant Snowdrop): Native to the Levant, it grows to 23 cm tall, flowers in January and February, and features large flowers with prominent green blotches on the inner tepals. It has supervolute vernation. Galanthus reginae-olgae: Found in Greece and Sicily, this species flowers in autumn before the leaves emerge. The leaves, which appear in spring, have a distinctive white stripe on their upper surface and exhibit applanate vernation. The genus Galanthus was first described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753, with Galanthus nivalis as the type species. The name Galanthus reflects the milk-like color of the flowers, while nivalis translates to of the snow. Snowdrops are sometimes confused with related genera such as Leucojum, which are larger and flower in spring or early summer, and Acis. Unlike Galanthus, Leucojum flowers have tepals of equal size. As of February 2012, the World Checklist of Selected Plant Families recognizes 19 species of Galanthus, with a 20th species, Galanthus panjutinii, identified later in 2012. This species, native to a small area in the northern Colchis region of Georgia and Russia, is classified as endangered due to habitat destruction, including the loss of one site during preparations for the 2014 Winter Olympics. The natural distribution of Galanthus spans Europe and the Middle East, from Spain and France in the west to Iran in the east. Some species, such as Galanthus nivalis, have become naturalized in other regions, including parts of northern Europe, Canada, and the United States. While often thought to be native to the British Isles, Galanthus nivalis was likely introduced in the early 16th century. Several Galanthus species are threatened in their natural habitats, and international trade of Galanthus plants, bulbs, or derivatives is regulated under CITES. Collecting bulbs from the wild is illegal in most countries without a permit. However, limited trade in wild-collected bulbs of three species (G. nivalis, G. elwesii, and G. woronowii) is permitted from Turkey and Georgia. Snowdrops are celebrated as a symbol of spring and are often cultivated in gardens, where they can form striking carpets of white flowers. Numerous gardens in the UK and Ireland open during the snowdrop season to showcase these displays. There are many cultivars of Galanthus, particularly of G. nivalis, G. plicatus, and G. elwesii, as well as hybrids. These cultivars vary in flower size, shape, markings, and flowering period, attracting dedicated collectors known as galanthophiles. Propagation of Galanthus is typically achieved through division of bulbs, either while the plants are actively growing (in the green) or after the leaves have withered. Seeds can also be sown when ripe or in spring. Advanced techniques, such as twin-scaling, are used by professional growers to rapidly increase stock. Galanthus contains active compounds with medicinal properties. One such compound, galantamine, is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that has been used in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease, although it is not a cure. Galantamine is also found in other plants, such as daffodils. Additionally, Galanthus contains a lectin known as Galanthus nivalis agglutinin (GNA), which has been studied for its potential applications in genetic modification and pest resistance. In popular culture, snowdrops have appeared in various literary and artistic works. For example, in the Russian fairy tale The Twelve Months by Samuil Marshak, snowdrops play a central role in the story. The flower is also featured in Hans Christian Andersen's short story The Snowdrop and in the musical Kiss Me, Kate by Cole Porter.
